source: Anderson (1991) The adaptive nature of human categorization (facts as described in Sanborn, Griffiths, Navarro 2010)
finding: Rational Model of Categorization (RMC). Category learning is Bayesian density estimation. Items are grouped into a flexible number of clusters. It covers both prototype and exemplar views. The number of clusters is chosen by the data, not fixed.
numbers: Prior on partitions uses a coupling parameter c: low c favours many small (exemplar-like) clusters, high c favours few large (prototype-like) clusters. Anderson used local MAP: each item is assigned once to its best cluster and never revised.
limits: Original paper is paywalled (no open copy found); facts come from the 2010 accepted manuscript, which I did read. Exact inference needs every partition of the items, which grows exponentially.
agent_relevance: A model for S2 REPRESENT: let the number of rules or sub-concepts grow with the data, and start simple. Each rule is a cluster; a surprising example should add a new one.

source: Sanborn, Griffiths, Navarro (2010) Rational approximations to rational models: alternative algorithms for category learning
finding: The RMC is the same as a Dirichlet process mixture model. Anderson's local MAP search is order-dependent and brittle. Gibbs sampling and particle filters approximate the same model better. A single-particle filter fits human data as well or better than local MAP.
numbers: Medin & Schaffer 1978 Exp 1, one training block: local MAP r=.87 at c=.3; particle filter M=100 r=.78, M=1 r=.77. Ten blocks: local MAP r=.95, M=1 r=.90, M=100 r=.93.
limits: Fits are correlations on a handful of transfer items. All three miss item 1110 (humans rated it differently from two items at the same distance).
agent_relevance: A rational model plus a cheap sampler can match people. One greedy pass over examples is order-sensitive; keep several candidate groupings.

source: Sanborn et al. (2010) - order effect and Smith & Minda fits
finding: Anderson & Matessa sorting study: 25 of 40 people (62.5%) sorted by the features that came first in training order (front-anchored 11/20, end-anchored 14/20). A single-particle filter gave the order effect on 63% of runs, M=100 particles on 52%, so one particle matches people best.
numbers: Smith & Minda 1998 Exps 1-3: single-particle filter had higher likelihood than local MAP in all 80 parameter settings; better on outlier items in 76 of 80. Best local MAP p=0.1, l=1, c=0.7; best M=1 p=1, l=0.5, c=0.5.
limits: The RMC statistical model itself has no order effect; order effects come only from the approximation. Fits are to group averages.
agent_relevance: Order effects are a feature of people and of any one-pass learner. Shuffle example order and aggregate before trusting a rule (fits G4).

source: Sanborn et al. (2010) - Shepard problems (Nosofsky et al. 1994 data) and brittleness of local MAP
finding: Nosofsky et al. (1994) fitted the RMC with local MAP (p=.488, l=.046, c=.318, exponent .93), SSD 0.182. Sanborn et al. found the second-best cluster can have a posterior ratio of 0.9997 to the best. With 64-bit numbers and ties shared, SSD rises to 0.32 and the difficulty ordering changes.
numbers: Parameter grid over 6 Shepard problems, 1000 reps: single-particle filter fit better than local MAP at 58% of settings; best SSD 0.24 against 0.31 for local MAP.
limits: A published rational-model fit depended on numeric precision. Treat reported fits of greedy clustering with care.
agent_relevance: Near-ties between candidate rules are common. Do not trust a hard argmax; keep near-tied candidates alive and test them.

source: MacLellan, Singaravadivelan, Lian, Wang, Langley (2026) A rational account of categorization based on information theory
finding: New rational theory: people learn a taxonomy (tree) of categories with maximal mutual information with the features (a category utility view), implemented as a Cobweb variant. It covers Hayes-Roth & Hayes-Roth 1977, Medin & Schaffer 1978 and Smith & Minda 1998.
numbers: Hayes-Roth 1977: Spearman rho 0.95-0.96 with human ratings. Medin & Schaffer Exp 1: Spearman .95 vs .91 for Anderson's RMC. Only two free parameters (max_nodes and a uniform-prior strength, set to 2.0 for Smith & Minda).
limits: Preprint, not peer reviewed. Only group averages were available. The prototype-to-exemplar transition appeared only with a hand-picked parameter (prior 2.0); below 0.6 it vanished and at 1 it looked like the HDP model. No ablations, no new human data.
agent_relevance: A tree of concepts (general nodes, specific leaves) gives both prototype and exemplar behaviour. A hierarchy of rules with exceptions is a sound shape for S2/S7.

source: MacLellan et al. (2026) - prototype-to-exemplar shift
finding: In Smith & Minda's non-linearly separable task, people first classify prototypes and standard items right, miss the exception items, and fix the exceptions only around segment 4 of 10. The Cobweb model shows the same flat-then-rise pattern (16 simulated participants, 10 segments).
numbers: Human pattern as reported via Griffiths et al. 2007 (16 participants, 10 segments, 14 stimuli).
limits: Qualitative match only; parameter chosen to make the effect appear.
agent_relevance: Exceptions to a rule are learned late. A rule that fits most examples early may still be wrong on a few; S7 should keep exceptions in a visible list, not drop them.

source: Love, Medin, Gureckis (2004) SUSTAIN: a network model of category learning
finding: SUSTAIN (a multiple-prototype clustering network) starts with one cluster per category and recruits a new cluster only on a surprising event (wrong label, or an item too far from every cluster). Five principles: simple first; similar items cluster; supervised and unsupervised learning use one mechanism; feedback pattern matters; clusters compete.
numbers: Fits six data sets. Modal cluster counts for Shepard types: Type I 2 clusters, Type II 4, Types III-V 6, Type VI 8. Difficulty tracks cluster count.
limits: Fits are to group means. The paper says some behaviours cannot be produced whatever the parameters. Recruitment is driven by the task, not only by environment statistics.
agent_relevance: A design for S2/S7: begin with the simplest rule; add a rule only on a real prediction error; difficulty equals the number of rules needed.

source: Love et al. (2004) - inference versus classification learning
finding: The same stimuli are learned differently depending on the question asked. Inference learning (predict a missing feature, label given) is faster for a linear structure. Classification (predict the label) is faster for a non-linear structure. SUSTAIN reproduces this.
numbers: Mean blocks to criterion, human (SUSTAIN): linear structure inference 6.5 (7.5), classification 12.3 (11.2); non-linear structure inference 27.4 (28.6), classification 10.4 (10.6). Criterion 90% over 3 blocks, max 30 blocks.
limits: Human data come from Yamauchi & Markman 1998 and Yamauchi, Love, Markman 2002. ALCOVE also fitted this table with a high initial weight on the label.
agent_relevance: The prediction task shapes the representation. For S2: ask the model to predict missing parts (inference) when structure is prototype-like, and to classify when it needs rules with exceptions.

source: Love et al. (2004) - item vs category learning, unsupervised learning
finding: Medin, Dewey, Murphy 1983: people learn a separate name per photograph (first-name) in fewer blocks than two category labels (last-name). SUSTAIN predicts this; ALCOVE could not. Billman & Knutson 1996: unsupervised learning is easier when features are inter-correlated. Medin et al. 1987: in free sorting people often sort on one dimension.
numbers: First-name vs last-name: blocks 7.1 (SUSTAIN 7.2) vs 9.7 (9.7); accuracy .84 (.85) vs .87 (.87); first-name accuracy 91% when scored by category. Billman & Knutson Exp 2: .62 vs .73 (SUSTAIN .66 vs .78); Exp 3 nonintercorrelated .66 (SUSTAIN .60).
limits: Group means from old studies; SUSTAIN misses part of Exp 3.
agent_relevance: People prefer one-dimension rules when sorting. An agent grouping unlabeled examples should expect, and check for, a single-feature shortcut.

source: Love et al. (2004) - contrast with the rational model
finding: SUSTAIN differs from Anderson's RMC: clusters form after prediction failures, not from statistics alone. It treats the queried dimension (the label) differently. It can build two different representations of one category depending on task. The RMC cannot.
numbers: No single number; the argument rests on the inference-vs-classification fit above.
limits: Authors compare their own model; no head-to-head quantitative test with the RMC in this paper.
agent_relevance: Supports a trigger rule: change the rule set only on a prediction failure (matches G1).

source: Mitchell, Keller, Kedar-Cabelli (1986) Explanation-based generalization: a unifying view
finding: EBG learns a general concept from ONE example plus a domain theory. Step 1 Explain: prove why the example fits the goal concept using the theory. Step 2 Generalise: regress the goal concept through the proof to get sufficient conditions in operational terms. The explanation separates relevant from irrelevant features.
numbers: Worked examples: SAFE-TO-STACK(x,y), CUP, a search-control problem, a schema example. Four inputs: goal concept, one training example, domain theory, operationality criterion.
quote: their ability to generalize from a single example follows from their ability to explain why the training example is a member of the concept
limits: Needs a complete, correct, tractable theory. No human data; a machine learning paper.
agent_relevance: Template for S2: explain why this example satisfies the goal using stated background facts, then keep only the features the explanation used. Check the explanation by code where possible (G2/G3).

source: Mitchell, Keller, Kedar-Cabelli (1986) - imperfect theories
finding: Three named failures when the theory is imperfect: incomplete (cannot prove the example), intractable (proof too costly, e.g. quantum physics for stacking), inconsistent (default and computed rules give two weights). They call for combining explanation-based with similarity-based methods.
numbers: Example: a weak economics theory marks 'cash on hand' as relevant to 'stocks that double' and 'middle initial of the president' as irrelevant.
limits: Stated as open problems in 1986.
agent_relevance: The agent's background knowledge is incomplete and sometimes inconsistent. Use it to rank features, then confirm on more examples; a single explanation is not proof.

source: Tenenbaum & Griffiths (2001) Generalization, similarity, and Bayesian inference
finding: Recasts Shepard's universal law of generalization as Bayesian inference over consequential regions. It extends to many examples and unifies set-theoretic (contrast, additive clustering) and spatial similarity models. Related: Tenenbaum 1999 Bayesian concept learning.
numbers: Abstract page only: BBS 24(4), 629-640. No numbers read.
limits: Only the abstract page was open (full text paywalled). Do not cite this line for numbers.
agent_relevance: Size principle idea: a narrow hypothesis that fits all examples is favoured over a broad one. Prefer the tightest rule that fits (S7).

source: Lee, Wills, Schlegelmilch (2026) Is generalization general? Predictive vs category learning (Open Mind)
finding: Tests Shepard's claim of universal generalization gradients by comparing category learning with predictive learning, same stimuli and procedure. When test procedures are equated, gradients are largely similar. Exp 2 shows some differences, explained by categories being mutually exclusive while outcomes are not.
numbers: Prolific, preregistered. Exp 1: 309 recruited, 277 analysed (cells 32-40). Exp 2: 348 recruited, 245 analysed (30 per cell).
limits: Online grey rectangles; one stimulus type. Many apparent differences came from test wording (absolute vs relative, test order).
agent_relevance: How a question is asked can fake a difference in what was learned. Keep the test prompt fixed when comparing rule sets.

source: REFRESH: a new approach to modeling dimensional biases in perceptual similarity and categorization (Psychological Review 2021)
finding: REFRESH is a pure family-resemblance (clustering) version of the RMC with a hierarchical prior. It learns from experience that clusters align with separable dimensions, and so explains dimensional biases (single-dimension categories are easier; the Shepard Type II advantage) without assuming separable dimensions.
numbers: Compared with Kurtz et al. 2012 (Exps 1, 2, 4: 64 trials each) and Love & Markman 2003 Exp 1 (128 trials). Type II advantage depends on the dimensions used and is absent for integral dimensions.
limits: I did not read the byline field. Fits were shown mostly as curves in the parts I read.
agent_relevance: Rules aligned with natural dimensions of the input are learned fast. Present examples in a form that exposes the right dimension (S1/S2).

source: Ellis (2023) Human-like few-shot learning via Bayesian reasoning over natural language
finding: An LLM (Codex code-davinci-002) proposes hypotheses in natural language; a prior and a likelihood reweight them (Bayesian). It fits human Number Game ratings with 50-100 proposed hypotheses; natural language beat Python as the hypothesis language; sampling from the prior alone fit poorly.
numbers: Number Game: averaged ratings of 8 humans; original model used over 5000 hypotheses. Logical concept learning (batches of 1-5 objects): R2 = .81 with 100 proposals per batch; within 3% of human accuracy; better than GPT-4 alone.
limits: Prior was tuned on human data. Fits are to averages of small groups. GPT-4 alone differed from humans.
agent_relevance: Closest published match to S2 plus S7: the LLM proposes rules, code weighs them against the examples. Supports using the model only to propose, and code to weigh (G5).

source: Wang, Zelikman, Poesia, Pu, Haber, Goodman (2024) Hypothesis search: inductive reasoning with language models
finding: GPT-4 writes natural-language hypotheses, turns each into Python, and tests it on the training examples. Explicit hypotheses lift ARC accuracy. Human-selected hypotheses help most.
numbers: 100 random ARC tasks: direct 17%, program only 23%, summarised hypotheses 30%, human-selected 33%, human-written (LARC) 45%. GPT-4 had a correct hypothesis for only 49 of 100 tasks; of those 33 (67%) gave a correct program. Chain-of-thought without programs: 19%. SyGuS 94.3% (89 tasks) with or without hypotheses.
limits: Top-1 accuracy, one model, 100-task subset. The hypothesis step is the bottleneck on ARC; on 1D-ARC and List Functions a right hypothesis almost always gave right code.
agent_relevance: Evidence for S2 and S3: sample many rules, verify each by running it on the examples, then select. Code check beat free-text reasoning (30% vs 19%).

source: Qiu, Jiang, Lu, Sclar et al. (2024) Phenomenal yet puzzling: testing inductive reasoning of language models with hypothesis refinement
finding: A propose-select-refine loop with a symbolic interpreter makes LMs strong rule inducers. But LMs cannot apply their own rules: using the LM itself as interpreter collapses accuracy.
numbers: ACRE raw accuracy 64% (IO) to 82.5% (T=3, N=5); ACRE task accuracy 28% to 59%. MiniSCAN task accuracy above 80% with a symbolic interpreter, near zero with the LM as interpreter. MiniARC task accuracy 14.6% symbolic vs 5.4% LM-interpreted (read from figure text).
limits: Table cells read from extracted text may be misaligned; trust the ranges and the interpreter gap, not each cell.
agent_relevance: The model can induce rules but should not be the one to apply or check them. Run the rule as code (G2, G5).

source: Qiu et al. (2024) - brittleness to noisy exemplars
finding: On List Functions, replacing 1-2 elements in 12.5%, 25% or 50% of 8 exemplars hurts the LM clearly, even for one noisy example; accuracy keeps falling as noise grows. A warning in the prompt only partly helps.
numbers: Noise levels 12.5/25/50% of 8 exemplars; exact accuracies are in a figure I did not transcribe.
limits: Specific to List Functions and 2023 models.
agent_relevance: A rule fitted to every given example (G3) can be wrong if one example is noisy. Allow a small named exception set and test it on held-out examples.

source: Zhu, Xue, Chen, Zhou, Schuurmans, Dai (2023) Large language models can learn rules (Hypotheses-to-Theories)
finding: Induction stage: the LLM writes and tests rules on training examples; rules that appear and lead to correct answers often enough enter a rule library. Deduction stage: the library goes into the prompt. Accuracy rises 10-30% absolute.
numbers: CLUTRR: +11.1 to +16.4 points over CoT/LtM. GPT-3.5 using GPT-4's rules: +27.2 on CLUTRR. List Functions: +18.5 to +18.7 raw, +10.2 to +14.5 task accuracy; GPT-3.5 task accuracy 34.4% with GPT-4 rules. HtT found over 85% of needed rules (Arithmetic). Random rules hurt.
limits: Needs a base model that can retrieve rules (little gain for GPT-3.5 on non-decimal arithmetic). Induction used up to 2,000 training examples. Gain mostly from fewer wrong-rule errors.
agent_relevance: Rules that survive many examples (an explicit library with counts) beat one-shot rules. Counting how often a rule is used and right is a code-side check for S7.

source: Han, Ransom, Perfors, Kemp (2023) Inductive reasoning in humans and large language models
finding: GPT-4 matches most human property-induction phenomena (similarity, typicality) but not premise non-monotonicity. Applying the similarity-coverage model to GPT-4's similarity ratings helps on some sets.
numbers: Exp 1: 792 argument pairs, 66 pairs per person, 11 phenomena. Exp 2: on individual arguments GPT-4 nearly matched the similarity-coverage model on specific arguments, GPT-3.5 on general ones; GPT-4 was uncorrelated with humans on single-premise mammal arguments.
limits: Humans did not show the diversity effect; single ratings are noisy; multi-premise general arguments had low reliability.
agent_relevance: LLM generalisation from examples to new cases is human-like on similarity but weak on how added examples change belief. Do not trust an LLM's belief shift when an example is added; compute it.

source: Binz et al. (2025) Centaur: a foundation model of human cognition
finding: Llama fine-tuned on Psych-101 (including Shepard-type and Medin categorisation, with the generalized context model as a baseline) predicts human choices better than cognitive models, also out of distribution (naturalistic category learning).
numbers: Response-time check: Centaur entropy conditional R2 .58 vs Llama .40 vs cognitive models .38.
limits: Category-specific numbers are in figures I did not transcribe. Fit to choices does not show a human-like mechanism.
agent_relevance: Human category-learning data are learnable by a model, but this gives no scaffold advice. Low direct relevance.

source: Medin & Schaffer (1978) Context theory of classification learning (as reported in Sanborn et al. 2010)
finding: Exp 1 used six training items with five binary features, and transfer items matched in distance to the category centre but unequal in nearness to specific instances. People rated by specific-instance similarity, not by centre alone. This is the base result for exemplar models over a single prototype.
numbers: Training items 11111, 10101, 01011, 00000, 01000, 10110 (last digit is the label).
limits: Second-hand. Item 1110 was rated higher than same-distance items, which no tested model captured.
agent_relevance: Specific examples count: an agent that keeps only an abstract rule loses information about near examples. Keep the examples next to the rule.

source: Smith & Minda (1998) Prototypes in the mist (as reported in Sanborn et al. 2010 and MacLellan et al. 2026)
finding: Early in learning, behaviour fits a prototype account; later it fits an exemplar account. In non-linearly separable categories, exceptions are misclassified early and then learned. Nosofsky & Zaki 2002 offer a rival reading: attention shifts from one dimension to all dimensions.
numbers: Griffiths et al. 2007 reproduced the data: 16 participants, 10 segments, 14 stimuli.
limits: Second-hand. The RMC, an HDP model and a Cobweb variant all reproduce the pattern, so the data do not separate them.
agent_relevance: Competing explanations fit the same curve. Do not read one rule-vs-exception curve as proof of a mechanism.

source: Hayes-Roth & Hayes-Roth (1977) Concept learning and the recognition and classification of exemplars (as reported in MacLellan et al. 2026)
finding: Classification accuracy rises as an item gets closer to the category prototype, even for prototypes never seen in training; frequently practised items are recognised better. Reviewing the prototypes before training raised accuracy but kept the same ranking of item types.
numbers: Only aggregate classification and recognition ratings were reported.
limits: Second-hand; no raw data.
agent_relevance: Unseen central cases can be classified best. For S7, test a rule built from examples on the central case it never saw.

source: Griffiths, Canini, Sanborn, Navarro (2007) Unifying rational models of categorization via the hierarchical Dirichlet process (as reported in Sanborn 2010 and MacLellan 2026)
finding: A hierarchical Dirichlet process model gives a continuum between prototype and exemplar representations. Its prior favours simple representations early, then the data overwhelm it, giving the Smith & Minda crossover.
numbers: No numbers read first-hand.
limits: Second-hand; I read two papers that describe it, not the paper.
agent_relevance: Same lesson as SUSTAIN: start simple, grow with data.

source: Shepard, Hovland, Jenkins (1961) six problem types, replicated by Nosofsky et al. (1994) (as reported in Love et al. 2004 and REFRESH)
finding: Eight items with three binary features are split into two categories in six ways. Learning order: Type I fastest, then II, then III-V, then VI slowest. Nosofsky et al. 1994 replicated with more people. The Type II (exclusive-or) advantage later proved to depend on the stimulus dimensions (Love & Markman 2003; Kurtz et al. 2012).
numbers: Clusters SUSTAIN needs: I 2, II 4, III-V 6, VI 8.
limits: Second-hand. Type II and III have equal Boolean complexity, so a pure complexity account is not enough.
agent_relevance: Rule complexity predicts difficulty, but not perfectly. Expect some rules of equal size to be harder for the model than others.
